meta.blurb: Born into slavery in Maryland, Frederick Douglass was never told his birthday and was forbidden to read. This is his own true story of how he taught himself, stood up to a cruel master and escaped to freedom, told in his own brave words.
meta.bible: Frederick Douglass: born Frederick Bailey into slavery in Talbot County, Maryland, about 1817 or 1818; the author of the Narrative, 1845; died in 1895. Harriet Bailey: his mother, who walked twelve miles at night to see him; she died when he was about seven. Betsy Bailey: his grandmother. Colonel Lloyd: the rich planter whose estate was the Great House Farm. Captain Anthony: Colonel Lloyd's manager and Frederick's first owner. Aunt Hester: Frederick's aunt, beaten by Captain Anthony. Mr Gore: a cruel overseer who shot Demby. Mr Severe: an overseer. Mr Hopkins: an overseer. Demby: an enslaved man shot by Mr Gore. Lucretia Auld: Captain Anthony's daughter, who was kind to Frederick. Thomas Auld: her husband and later Frederick's owner at St Michaels; mean and fond of religion. Hugh Auld: Thomas's brother, who lived in Baltimore. Sophia Auld: Hugh's wife, who first taught Frederick the alphabet. Edward Covey: the farmer known as a breaker of slaves, 1833. William Freeland: a fairer farmer who hired Frederick in 1834. Sandy Jenkins: an enslaved man with a free wife, who gave Frederick a root. David Ruggles: a Black abolitionist in New York. Anna Murray: a free woman of Baltimore who became Frederick's wife. Nathan Johnson: his host in New Bedford, who suggested the name Douglass. William Lloyd Garrison: the editor of The Liberator and the writer of the preface. Wendell Phillips: a campaigner who wrote a letter for the book. Abraham Lincoln: the President. Maryland. Baltimore. Wye. Easton. St Michaels. Chesapeake Bay. Georgia. New York. New Bedford. Massachusetts. Nantucket. Lynn. Ireland. Britain. Washington. Great House Farm. The Columbian Orator: a schoolbook of speeches. The Liberator: an antislavery newspaper. The North Star: Douglass's newspaper, 1847. The Lady of the Lake: a poem by Sir Walter Scott. Methodist. Christianity. Bible. Tuckahoe. Civil War. Black. Easter. Christmas. Georgia. Voice and tone: serious, dignified and clear; truthful and never graphic; cruelty is stated plainly and briefly with no gore; the writer admires Douglass's courage.

beats.scene: A small boy looks at a closed door in a dim hall

beats.scene: A frightened boy peers from behind a door into a barn

beats.scene: An angry man points at his wife while a boy listens at the door

beats.scene: A boy reads a thick book sitting on a wooden crate on a dockside

beats.scene: A woman's face grows stern as she stands over a boy with a book
beats.summary: Sophia Auld, who had been so kind, becomes harsh and watchful, changed by the power slavery gives its owners.

beats.scene: A boy reads the word abolition in a newspaper under a street lamp

A1A2: A famous writer, William Lloyd Garrison, begins the book with a short letter.
In 1845 Frederick Douglass wrote his own story, with real names and places.
Frederick Douglass was born a slave in Maryland, but he did not know his birthday.
Frederick's mother lived far away, but she walked at night to see him.
Frederick never knew who his father was, but people said he was a white man.
His grandmother, Betsy Bailey, took care of him until he was six.
Colonel Lloyd owned a huge farm with a great house at the centre.
The workers sang loudly on the road, but their songs were sad.
As a boy, Frederick saw his aunt Hester beaten, and he was very afraid.
The children had little food, few clothes and no beds in winter.
The bosses in the fields were hard men, and nobody stopped them.
A man told the truth to Colonel Lloyd, and he was sold far away.
Mrs Lucretia Auld was kind, and she sent Frederick to Baltimore.
In Baltimore, Mrs Sophia Auld was kind to him, as no one had been.
Mrs Auld began to teach Frederick the letters of the alphabet.
Mr Auld stopped the lessons, but Frederick learned something important from his anger.
Frederick gave bread to poor boys, and they helped him learn to read.
He practised his writing alone when the Aulds were away from the house.
At twelve, Frederick bought a book of speeches and read it again and again.
Mrs Auld changed, and she became stern and cold to Frederick.
In a newspaper, Frederick found a new word, abolition, and learned its meaning.
Two Irish men on the docks told Frederick to run away to the north.
After his old master died, Frederick returned to the plantation to be counted.
His grandmother, who had worked all her life, was left alone in old age.
Thomas Auld gave Frederick too little food, and he was often hungry.
Thomas Auld joined a church, but he became even harder on his slaves.
Frederick began a Sunday school and taught other slaves how to read.
In 1833 Frederick was sent to a hard farmer named Edward Covey.
On Sundays, Frederick watched the ships on the bay and dreamed of freedom.
One hot day Frederick fell ill in the field and could not work.
In the woods, a kind man named Sandy gave Frederick a special root.
On Monday, Frederick fought back against Covey, and Covey gave up.
In 1834 Frederick went to William Freeland, a fairer man, and taught again.
Slaves had a few days of rest at Christmas, and masters watched them closely.
In 1835 Frederick and some friends made a plan to escape.
Someone told the masters about the plan, and the men were arrested.
In the shipyard, some white workers attacked Frederick, because he was Black.
Frederick learned to build ships well, but he had to give away his wages.
On 3 September 1838, Frederick left Baltimore and escaped to the north.
Frederick reached New York, but he felt afraid and very much alone.
Anna Murray came to New York, and she and Frederick got married.
In New Bedford, Frederick took a new name, Douglass, to stay safe.
In New Bedford, Frederick found work on the docks and was paid well.
Frederick read The Liberator, and its words about freedom gave him great hope.
In 1841, Frederick spoke in public about slavery for the first time.
In a last part, Frederick wrote about religion and slavery.
Frederick signed his book in April 1845 and hoped it would help end slavery.
The book sold very well, and Douglass travelled to Britain and Ireland.
Douglass wrote for newspapers, spoke across the country, and met President Lincoln.
Today people all over the world still read the Narrative of Frederick Douglass.
B1B2: The book opens with a letter by William Lloyd Garrison, a famous campaigner against slavery. He remembers hearing Frederick Douglass speak for the first time in 1841, and he has never forgotten it.
Frederick Douglass published his Narrative in 1845, and the title page says it was written by himself. He used real names and places, because he wanted readers to be able to check every fact.
Frederick was born in Talbot County, Maryland, and the book says that he never knew his exact age. Enslaved children were not told their birthdays, and he thought he was born in 1817 or 1818.
Frederick's mother, Harriet Bailey, was sent to work on a farm twelve miles away. She walked that distance at night, after a day's work, only to lie beside her son for a few hours.
Frederick never knew his father, though he was told that he was a white man. The law said that a child took the status of its mother, so he was born into slavery.
Frederick was raised by his grandmother, Betsy Bailey, in a small cabin. When he was about six years old, he was taken to live on the plantation of Colonel Lloyd.
Colonel Lloyd's farm was so big that it was like a small village, with its own shops and workers. Captain Anthony, who owned Frederick, was in charge of managing it.
As they walked to collect their monthly food, the workers sang loudly and often. Frederick says that people thought the songs showed happiness, but he later understood that they spoke of sorrow.
One morning Frederick watched in terror as his aunt Hester was beaten by Captain Anthony. It was the first time he understood what slavery really meant, and he never forgot it.
Children on the plantation ate corn porridge from a wooden trough, like farm animals. They wore only a rough shirt, had no bed, and in winter their feet cracked from the cold.
Some overseers were cruel, and others were just proud of their power. Mr Gore shot an enslaved man named Demby, and nothing happened to him, because a slave's life counted for so little.

One man told Colonel Lloyd honestly that he was not treated well, and he was soon sold to a trader going south. After that, the enslaved learned to say that their master was kind, even when it was untrue.

Lucretia Auld, the daughter of Captain Anthony, was kind to Frederick and sometimes gave him bread. When he was about eight, she arranged for him to go to Baltimore, and he was told to wash himself before he went.
In Baltimore, Frederick lived with Hugh and Sophia Auld. Sophia had never owned a slave before, and she treated the boy with a kindness that astonished him.
Sophia Auld began to teach Frederick the alphabet, and soon he could read a few short words. She was proud of him and told her husband how quickly he learned.
Hugh Auld told his wife to stop at once, because a slave who could read would want to be free. Frederick, listening nearby, understood for the first time that reading was the way out of slavery.

Frederick took bread out into the street and shared it with hungry white boys, who taught him letters in return. He also copied letters from the wood in the shipyard and challenged other boys to write better than him.
When the Aulds were out, Frederick took out an old copybook belonging to their son. He copied each line over and over until his handwriting was as neat as the printed example.

When he was about twelve, Frederick earned a little money and bought a book called The Columbian Orator. In it he found speeches about freedom and a conversation in which an enslaved man argued so well that his master let him go.
Sophia, who had been so gentle, slowly changed and began to be cold and strict. Frederick understood that slavery harmed the slaveholder as well as the slave, because it made a good person cruel.
Frederick read in a newspaper about people called abolitionists, who wanted to end slavery. At first, learning more only made him sadder, and he sometimes wished that he were still ignorant.
One day, two Irish workers on the docks asked Frederick if he was a slave for life. When he said yes, they told him to run away to the free states, where he would find friends.
After Captain Anthony died, Frederick was sent back to the plantation to be valued, along with all the property. He stood in line next to horses, sheep and pigs, and was counted as one more animal.

His grandmother had served the family faithfully for her whole life, and all her children and grandchildren had been taken from her. When she grew old, she was left in a small hut in the woods with nobody to care for her.
At St Michaels, Frederick was owned by Thomas Auld, who was mean and fed his slaves very little. The boy was so hungry that he sometimes begged and even took food from the neighbours.
Thomas Auld went to a religious camp meeting and said that he had found God. Frederick hoped that his master would become kinder, but he became even crueller and used the Bible to excuse his actions.
On Sundays, Frederick taught other enslaved people to read the Bible in a small school. A mob of white men, some of them church leaders, broke up the class and told him to stop.

In January 1833 Frederick was hired out for a year to a farmer named Edward Covey, who was known as a breaker of slaves. Covey worked him from before dawn until after dark, and Frederick was whipped for small mistakes.
On Sundays, Frederick sat by Chesapeake Bay and watched the white sails of ships. He spoke to them in his heart, saying that they were free and he was in chains.
In August, Frederick fell ill from the heat and collapsed in the field. Covey hit him, so he ran seven miles to ask Thomas Auld for help, but his master told him to go back.
Frederick hid in the woods for a night, and then met an enslaved man named Sandy Jenkins, who gave him a root. Sandy said that if he carried it on his right side, no white man could hurt him.
On Monday morning Covey tried to tie him up, but Frederick resisted, and they fought for nearly two hours. Covey finally stopped, and he never tried to beat Frederick again.
In 1834 Frederick was hired out to William Freeland, who treated his workers better than Covey had. Frederick started another Sunday school, and this time more than twenty people came to learn.

At Christmas the slaveholders gave their workers a few days off, and they encouraged them to drink a lot. Douglass thought this was a clever trick, because it made freedom seem like a kind of foolish drunkenness.
In 1835 Frederick and five friends planned to escape by canoe up Chesapeake Bay and then walk north. Frederick wrote passes for each man, saying that he had permission to travel.
Before they could escape, the plot was discovered, and the six men were arrested. Frederick spent several days in jail, but then Thomas Auld took him out and sent him back to Baltimore.

Frederick was sent to learn the work of a ship's caulker, but white carpenters did not want Black men to have skilled work. Several of them attacked him, and one injured his eye so badly that it swelled shut.
Frederick soon became a skilled caulker and earned good wages. Every Saturday evening, however, he had to place all of his money in Hugh Auld's hand.
On 3 September 1838, Frederick escaped from slavery and travelled north to freedom. He does not tell us how he did it, because he did not want to help slaveholders stop other people from escaping.
In New York, Frederick was free but felt lonely and afraid of slave catchers. A kind man named David Ruggles, who helped fugitives, gave him a place to stay.
Anna Murray was a free woman who lived in Baltimore, and she came to join Frederick in New York. They were married there within days, and they travelled on to the port of New Bedford.
To avoid slave catchers, Frederick changed his name several times. At last his host, Nathan Johnson, suggested Douglass, a name from a poem by Sir Walter Scott, and he kept it for life.

In New Bedford, Frederick found work on the docks and kept his own wages for the first time. He was surprised to find that people in the North, where there was no slavery, lived in beautiful houses and were not poor.
Douglass began to read a newspaper called The Liberator, which was edited by William Lloyd Garrison. He says that its fierce words against slavery gave him fresh strength and hope.
In August 1841, at an antislavery meeting on the island of Nantucket, Frederick was asked to speak. He was nervous, but his story moved the whole audience, and Garrison himself praised him.

In an appendix at the end of the book, Douglass explains that he is not against true Christianity. He is against the religion of slaveholders, who go to church and pray while they treat other people cruelly.
Douglass finishes his book by saying that he hopes it will help people understand the evils of slavery. He signs it Frederick Douglass, in Lynn, Massachusetts, on 28 April 1845.

The Narrative sold quickly and made Douglass famous, but it also made it easy for his old master to find him. He travelled to Britain and Ireland, where friends raised money to buy his legal freedom in 1846.

After his return, Douglass started a newspaper called The North Star in 1847. He also supported women's rights, and during the Civil War he met President Abraham Lincoln and urged him to let Black men fight.
Today the Narrative is still read in schools and homes around the world. It shows that learning to read helped one man change his life, and that free people must never forget how others were treated.
C1C2: The book opens with a preface by William Lloyd Garrison, the best-known newspaper editor among those who fought to end slavery. He recalls the evening in 1841 when he first heard Frederick Douglass speak, and he describes how the whole audience seemed to hold its breath. Garrison urges every reader to treat the story that follows as the plain truth, told by the one man who lived it.

In 1845 Douglass published his Narrative, and its title page proudly states that it was written by himself, a claim that many readers found hard to believe. Because he had escaped from slavery only a few years earlier, he took a serious risk by naming real people and real places, yet he insisted that the truth must be told in full. Wendell Phillips, another leading campaigner, wrote a letter praising the book's honesty and warning that the facts would shock the nation.

Douglass begins by explaining that he was born in Talbot County, Maryland, in a place called Tuckahoe, and that he has no accurate knowledge of his own age. Slave owners rarely allowed the enslaved to keep a record of their birthdays, and he tells us that he believed himself to have been born around 1817 or 1818. Even this simple fact, which most free children take for granted, had been withheld from him.

Frederick was separated from his mother, Harriet Bailey, when he was still an infant, and she was hired out to a farm some twelve miles away. After a full day in the fields she would walk that distance in the dark, arrive in the small hours, and lie beside her sleeping son until she had to hurry back before dawn. She died when he was about seven, and he was not allowed to be with her at the end.

Douglass never learned for certain who his father was, but he was told that the man was white, and it was whispered that he might even have been his master. Under the law of the time a child followed the condition of its mother, which meant that children of enslaved women were enslaved no matter who their fathers were. He points out that this rule gave slaveholders both a profit and a way to hide what they had done.

Until the age of about six, Frederick lived with his grandmother, Betsy Bailey, in a small cabin, and he knew nothing of the world beyond her care. Then one day she walked with him many miles to the plantation of Colonel Lloyd, where he was to live from that time forward. He recalls that, when he finally understood he was being left there, he threw himself on the ground and cried.

Colonel Lloyd's estate was so large that it resembled a small village, with its own blacksmiths, weavers and shoemakers, all surrounding a magnificent house known as the Great House Farm. Captain Anthony, who owned Frederick and was the colonel's chief manager, held authority over hundreds of men, women and children. To the young boy, who had never seen anything bigger than his grandmother's cabin, the place seemed enormous and a little frightening.

As the workers walked to the Great House Farm to collect their monthly supplies, they sang, sometimes wildly, sometimes tenderly, in words that often made little sense. Outsiders imagined that the singers must be happy, but Douglass insists that the songs were the cry of hearts heavy with sorrow, and that tears were the truest response to them. He confesses that hearing them still affected him more deeply than any book he had read about slavery.

Early one morning the young Frederick hid in a closet and watched, in horror, as Captain Anthony beat his aunt Hester for a trivial offence. He tells the reader that this was his first real glimpse of the cruelty on which slavery depended, and that he felt as though he had been taken through a gateway into hell. The scene taught him a lesson he would never forget, and he wrote about it plainly, without describing the worst.

The children on Colonel Lloyd's estate were given cornmeal mush, which was poured into a long wooden trough and eaten with bare hands or pieces of oyster shell, like feed for pigs. They wore a single coarse shirt, owned no bed, and slept on the cold ground with only a sack for a blanket. In winter, Douglass recalls, the frost cracked his feet so badly that a pen could have been laid in the cuts.

The overseers who ruled the fields varied in character, though few were kind, and Douglass names a Mr Severe, a Mr Hopkins and a Mr Gore, whose pride made him the most feared of them all. When an enslaved man named Demby ran into a creek to escape a whipping and refused to come out, Gore shot him dead before the other workers' eyes. Nobody ever called him to account, and the white planters of the district accepted his explanation without a question.

Douglass recounts how a stranger once asked an enslaved man whether Colonel Lloyd was a good master, and the man answered honestly that he was not. Soon afterwards the man was sold to a trader bound for Georgia, which was feared by the enslaved as the worst of fates, and everyone on the estate understood the lesson. From then on, the enslaved learned to praise their masters in public, even though they knew very well that it was a lie.

One of the few kind people on the plantation was Lucretia Auld, the captain's daughter, who sometimes gave Frederick bread when he was hungry. When he was about eight years old she arranged for him to be sent to Baltimore, to serve in the household of her brother-in-law, Hugh Auld. Frederick scrubbed himself clean for the journey, in return for his first pair of trousers, and he counted the days until he could leave.

In Baltimore, Frederick joined the household of Hugh Auld and his wife, Sophia, who had never before owned a slave and had worked for her living as a weaver. She spoke to him gently, gave him decent food, and treated him almost like a child of her own, a thing he had not known in all his years on the plantation. Douglass remembers the move as the first stroke of good fortune in his life, and he sees it as the hand of Providence.

Sophia was a kind and curious woman, and without a second thought she began to teach the boy his letters, and then to spell short words from the primer. Frederick learned so quickly that she told her husband about it with real pride, never imagining how he would respond. Neither of them realised that a small act of kindness was about to grow into the most important event of his life.

When Hugh Auld heard what his wife had been doing, he ordered her to stop immediately, declaring that a slave who learned to read would soon become discontented and impossible to manage. Frederick, who was listening, felt a sudden light break upon his mind, for he understood in that moment what the white man most feared and what the enslaved most needed. From that day, he says, he knew the pathway from slavery to freedom, and he never lost sight of it.

Determined to learn despite the ban, Frederick carried bread into the street and shared it with poor white boys, who were hungry for it and happy to give him lessons in return. He also copied the letters marked on the timber in the shipyards, and he challenged other boys to prove that they could write better than he could, so that they would show him the correct shapes. Slowly and patiently, he put together the lessons of the street, one letter at a time, until he could read.

Whenever the household was out, Frederick took down the old copybook that belonged to the young master and copied the model handwriting line by line, over and over, until the words began to look like his own. His secret practice lasted for several years, and in the end he could write as well as any boy of his age in the city. It was a skill that no one had given him, and no one could ever take away.

With a few coins earned by shining boots, Frederick bought a schoolbook called The Columbian Orator, and he read it until its pages were worn at the edges. In it he found speeches in praise of liberty, and a dialogue in which a slave argues with his owner so persuasively that the master gives him his freedom. These words gave shape to feelings that he had had since childhood, and they made him hate slavery more than ever.

Sophia Auld, who had once been so gentle, gradually grew cold and suspicious, snatching the book from his hands when she found him reading and warning him that it was against the rules. Douglass observes that this was not her natural character but the result of the power that slavery gave to an owner, a power that slowly spoiled every heart that held it. He draws the lesson that the system harmed the master as well as the enslaved.

While reading a newspaper, Frederick met the word abolition, and he searched for its meaning until he discovered that there were people in the free states who wished to bring slavery to an end. His new knowledge brought hope, but it also brought torment, because it made the horror of his own situation more vivid, and there were times when he envied the ignorant. Reading had given him a clear view of the chain, but not the key to unlock it.

One day, while Frederick was helping two Irish labourers unload a boat, they asked him whether he was a slave for life, and he answered that he was. They were deeply moved, and they urged him to escape to the free states in the north, where, they promised, he would find friends and be able to work for himself. He thanked them, but he privately resolved to be cautious, for he had learned that even a friendly face could turn out to be a trap.

When his owner, Captain Anthony, died, Frederick was summoned back to the plantation so that the estate could be divided among the heirs, and he saw his family again after years of absence. The assessors weighed up men, women and children together with horses, sheep and pigs, as though all were of the same kind. He remarks that nothing could have taught him the meaning of slavery more clearly than this long afternoon of being valued.

Douglass pauses in his narrative to describe the fate of his grandmother, who had served her owners faithfully for decades and had raised many children, all of whom had been taken from her one by one. When she grew too old to work, she was sent to live in a small hut in the woods, where she was left to look after herself and to face her last days alone. This was, he says, the reward that a lifetime of loyalty earned under slavery.

At St Michaels, on the Maryland shore, Frederick came under the control of Thomas Auld, a mean man who fed his household of slaves so poorly that they often went hungry. Douglass, who was now about fifteen, was sometimes reduced to begging from neighbours' kitchens or stealing a little corn, and he insists that hunger can drive an honest man to take what he needs. Master Thomas, he adds, was rich enough, but he was rich in everything except generosity.

In August 1832, Thomas Auld attended a religious camp meeting and announced that he had been converted, and Frederick hoped that his master might now become kinder. Instead, Auld grew even more harsh, quoting the Bible to justify his orders and praying loudly at the very moments when he was treating his servants unfairly. It was Douglass's first clear lesson in the difference between professing religion and practising it.

Frederick secretly started a Sunday school, where he taught other enslaved men and women how to read the Bible, and they came eagerly, even though they risked punishment. After a few weeks a group of white men, some of them church leaders and class-leaders, burst in with sticks and broke up the meeting, warning the pupils never to return. Even this violence could not dim his belief that a mind once opened will never willingly be closed.

In January 1833 Thomas Auld hired out Frederick for a year to Edward Covey, a poor farmer who had a reputation for breaking the spirit of troublesome slaves. For six months Douglass was driven from before dawn until long after dark, in all weathers, and was punished for the smallest mistakes, until he felt that his body, his mind and his courage were wearing out. His love of reading, he says, faded, and the light of his intellect grew dim.

On Sundays, the only time he could rest, Frederick would sit beside Chesapeake Bay and watch the white sails of ships gliding toward distant harbours. In a passage that has been quoted ever since, he addresses them aloud, telling the ships that they are loosed from their moorings and free, while he remains fast in his chains. Yet even in despair he told himself that he would one day be free, and that the day would come.

One burning day in August, Frederick collapsed in the field from heat and exhaustion, and Covey struck him instead of helping, leaving him hurt and dazed. Frederick walked some seven miles to St Michaels and begged Thomas Auld to protect him, but his master only said that Covey was a good man and ordered him to return. It was a bitter disappointment, but it also taught him that nobody would defend him except himself.

After hiding in the woods overnight, Frederick met Sandy Jenkins, a friendly enslaved man who offered him shelter and a meal, and advised him to carry a certain root in his right pocket. Sandy swore that, with this charm, no white man would be able to strike him, and although Douglass did not believe in such things, he took it, so as not to offend. Then he walked back towards the farm, ready to face whatever the morning would bring.

On Monday morning Covey tried to tie him up for a beating, but Frederick, who had decided he would not be flogged again, caught hold of him, and the two men struggled for nearly two hours. At last the exhausted farmer gave up, and he never laid a hand on Frederick again during the remaining six months of the year. The fight, Douglass says, was the turning point of his life, for it taught him that a man who will not be a slave is already half free.

In 1834 Frederick was hired out to William Freeland, who was a gentleman by comparison with Covey and who gave his workers enough to eat and time to rest. Encouraged, Douglass opened another Sunday school, and some twenty or more eager pupils came to learn to read, often walking long distances in secret. He says that these were the happiest friendships of his life, formed among people who risked everything for a few lessons.

At Christmas the slaveholders allowed their workers a week of holiday, and many of them encouraged the men to drink and to dance until they were thoroughly drunk. Douglass explains that this was a cunning policy, intended to leave the enslaved with such a disgust for their own behaviour that they would fear to be free and would welcome a return to work. These holidays, he says, were safety valves that prevented the pressure of resentment from becoming dangerous.

Early in 1835, Frederick and five friends secretly agreed to escape on the Saturday night before Easter, paddling a canoe up Chesapeake Bay and then following the North Star on foot. Douglass wrote a pass for each of them, claiming that the bearer had permission to go to Baltimore, and for weeks the group went about their duties as though nothing were different. They knew the risk, and they accepted it, because they had come to believe that bondage was worse than death.

On the morning of the planned escape, the conspiracy was discovered, probably through an informer, and the men were arrested and marched into the town. Frederick spent several days in the jail at Easton, expecting to be sold south, but Thomas Auld, to his surprise, took him out and sent him back to Baltimore to live again with Hugh Auld. The other men were eventually released, and Douglass notes with relief that nobody was sold.

Back in Baltimore, Frederick was sent to a shipyard to learn the trade of caulking, which meant sealing the seams between planks so that vessels would stay afloat. White carpenters, who feared that free Black workers would drive down their wages, turned on him, and a gang of them beat him until one eye was almost closed. Hugh Auld, surprisingly, took his side and sought justice, but no white witness would speak, and so the case was dropped.

Within a short time Frederick had become so skilled that he was earning the highest wages paid to any caulker in the yard, and he worked with pride. Yet every Saturday evening he had to place the entire sum in Hugh Auld's hand, receiving at best a few coppers in return, and he declares plainly that this was nothing less than robbery. The more he earned for his master, the more he longed to keep it for himself.

On 3 September 1838, Frederick finally made his break for freedom, and within a day he had left the slave state of Maryland behind him. In his book he deliberately gives no details of the route or the methods, since he does not wish to reveal secrets that would help slaveholders block the paths of others who were still trying to follow him. He writes that the day was the most important in his life, and that it ended in a feeling of joy and fear.

Arriving in New York, Frederick felt free and fearful in equal measure, since he had no money, no friends and no way of telling whom he could trust. He wandered the streets for a time, sleeping among barrels, until a sailor led him to David Ruggles, a Black abolitionist who ran a hiding place for fugitives. Douglass felt, as he tells us, like a person who had escaped from a den of hungry lions.

Frederick sent word to Baltimore, and Anna Murray, a free woman to whom he was engaged, came to join him in New York, to start a household with him. They were married within days by a Black minister, and soon afterwards they travelled to New Bedford, Massachusetts, where Ruggles had told them they would find work and friends. The newly married couple arrived with almost no money, but they had something worth more than gold.

To make it harder for slave catchers to trace him, Frederick had already changed his name more than once, but he now gave up the name of Bailey for good. His host in New Bedford, Nathan Johnson, who was an admirer of Sir Walter Scott's poem The Lady of the Lake, suggested the name Douglass, after one of its heroes, and he took it gladly. It was a name that would soon be known on both sides of the Atlantic.

In New Bedford, Douglass worked on the docks, sawed wood and shovelled coal, and for the first time in his life he was paid for what he did and allowed to keep it. He was astonished to find that a town without slaves was so prosperous, with fine houses and well-fed families, for he had been taught that slavery was the source of wealth. Seeing Black and white workers earn their living together, he gained a new conviction about what free labour could achieve.

Soon after reaching New Bedford, Douglass subscribed to The Liberator, the antislavery paper edited by William Lloyd Garrison, and he read it as eagerly as a starving man eats. Its fierce and unflinching attacks on the slaveholders awakened in him a new energy, and he felt that his own thoughts had at last been given words. He says that the paper became, in a sense, his political education and his greatest source of courage.

In August 1841, at an antislavery convention on the island of Nantucket, Douglass was unexpectedly invited to tell his story to the audience, and he rose with a trembling voice and a racing heart. He spoke only a few minutes, but his words made such an impression that William Lloyd Garrison followed him to the platform and used his story as a text. Before long, the anti-slavery society had offered him a job as a lecturing agent.

In the Appendix, Douglass makes clear that his anger is not directed against religion itself, but against the hypocrisy of those who preached Christian love on Sundays and bought and sold human beings on Mondays. He distinguishes sharply between the Christianity of Christ and the Christianity of the land, which he finds not only different but opposed, and he argues that the one is pure and peaceable while the other is corrupt. It is some of the angriest and most eloquent writing in the whole book.

Douglass closes his Narrative with a modest hope, that his little book may help to shed light on the American slave system and hasten the day of its destruction. He signs it Frederick Douglass, Lynn, Massachusetts, 28 April 1845, and sends the pages to the printer knowing that the publication could expose him to capture and return. It was a risk that he judged worth taking, because the cause was larger than any single person.

The Narrative was published in 1845 and sold quickly, but its fame had an unwelcome side effect, because it revealed the name of Douglass's former owner and made his recapture more likely. On the advice of his friends he travelled to Ireland and Britain, where he lectured for nearly two years, and a group of British supporters raised about 150 pounds to buy his legal freedom in 1846. He returned to the United States as a free man in the eyes of the law.

After his return he founded his own newspaper, The North Star, in 1847, and went on to become the most famous Black man in America, speaking against slavery and for the rights of women. During the Civil War he urged President Abraham Lincoln to let Black men serve as soldiers, and he later held several public offices. He died in Washington in 1895, still working for justice after more than fifty years of public life.

Today the Narrative is regarded as one of the great works of American literature, read in classrooms around the world and admired for its clarity, its courage and its dignity. Above all, it shows that a determined mind, armed with the ability to read and to write, is more dangerous to injustice than any army. Douglass had shown his readers that freedom begins in the mind, and that no chain can hold a person who has learned to think.
